newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: World credit system faces new risks - S&P official.
newsitem.headline: World credit system faces new risks - S&P official.

text.p: Free market reform and growing credit markets have brought heady economic growth but are leading the world financial system into risky, unchartered territory, a top Standard & Poor's official said on Tuesday.

"This explosive growth and evolution of financial markets is not cost-free or risk-free," Hendrik Kranenburg, executive vice-president of Standard & Poor's Ratings Services, told a bankers convention in Argentina.
"The factors that contribute to higher sovereign credit quality also heighten the credit risks encountered by banks, utilities, corporates and other market sectors," he said.
Privatization, which may help governments bolster their sovereign risks, is also providing new challenges for the financial markets.

"Utilities, telecommunications and transportation stand out as sectors where, in country after country, the abolition of old quasi-monopolies and government protection is raising the risk profile," Kranenburg said.
Lending is also becoming a more complicted business.
"Project finance, asset-backed securities, future flow transactions and other forms of structured finance make the analysis of creditworthiness all the more complicated," he said.
One of the bigger coming changes to the world's financial topography will take place with the implementation of a single currency within the European Union, said Kranenburg.

"At Standard & Poor's we believe that credit spreads will replace currency cross-rates as the fundamental basis for valuing fixed-income investments acorss the new Euro-currency zone. This will be true even for those countries that don't join EMU in the first wave."
While S&P recently upgraded China, murky laws and practices still conceal much data vital for hordes of foreign investors lured to Asia's emerging giant, Kranenburg said.

"I expect it will be quite a few years before open disclosure of financial information and risk-based lending decisions are adopted. As a consequence, the risk of investment in China is difficult to gauge, and there will be unknown consequences for banks and other enterprises that do business there," he said.
Latin America, traditionally a racy corner of the globe for risk-raters, has not entirely buried its past despite big steps towards fiscal probity and economic predictability.

"There is still a genuine potential for volatility. Trade balances and capital flows remain a challenge even for the most fiscally conservative nations," Kranenburg said, "And at the heart of many sovereign credit situations are political issues - the future party developments in Mexico, the policy outlook beyond the current presidential elections in Brazil, the ongoing dynamic of consitutional reform in Chile."

Last year even the United States cast a shadow over what was once considered one of risk-ratings surest bets, with the government's showdown with Congress recently raising the prospect of a U.S. government debt default.

"The whole exercise seems to have had the beneficial effect of a renewed appreciation among investors everywhere that governments can and sometimes will default. There is, in fact, a need to think about the unthinkable. To measure defualt risks," Kranenburg said.
